# Feedback, Verification, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"*
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's note.** Dijkstra's warning separates a check from the stronger claim
someone might attach to it. Passing tests supports only the conditions and
behaviors the tests exercised. A failed test can still decisively contradict a
bounded claim.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What signal came back, what does it say about a named action, artifact,
assumption, or result, and what should the project learn or change because of
it?
:::

Feedback is a returned signal about an action, artifact, assumption, or result.
It may report a measurement, expose a failure, localize a cause, challenge a
rationale, or leave a question unresolved. Feedback can justify a recorded
update only when the record names what produced it, what it refers to, when it
was obtained, and what kind of update it supports.

Architecture studies combine empirical measurements, formal results,
simulation, physical analysis, model predictions, reviews, and field
observations. These signals do not share one meaning of *pass*, one type of
uncertainty, or one scope. The chapter problem is to qualify each return for
the property it can address, compare like with like, expose what remains
unchecked, and route the result without letting the signal decide its own use.

The problem appears in the intentionally incomplete Lighthouse cache record
from @tbl-lighthouse-execution-record. It reports SRAM and cycle-level returns
for the 2, 3, and 4\ MB candidates, one stale-state attempt, two later clean
3\ MB attempts, and an exhausted cycle-level budget.

The record also says what is missing. It does not retain exact translated
inputs, tool and model versions, parser status, raw artifact identities, frame
identifiers, reset state, or attempt-level attribution for the aggregate 3\ MB
values. Every numerical value came from the constructed teaching trace
introduced in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces rather than a live
project run. A complete-looking table could hide those limitations, but it
could not repair them.

This incomplete record shows why feedback needs qualification. A returned
number is not automatically a measurement. A measurement is not automatically
a valid comparison. A valid comparison supports only the property, candidate,
conditions, and check scope that produced it. AI makes these distinctions more
important because it can produce and score candidates faster, search directly
against imperfect proxies, and generate explanations that sound more certain
than the measurements allow. It does not change what an architecture result
must contain.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Classify feedback by its source, form, timing, locality, and quality before
  using it to guide learning or revision.
- Distinguish execution status from measurement status and identify the fields
  a returned value needs before it can enter a comparison.
- Build a matched comparison with a named candidate, comparator, quantity,
  unit, conditions, uncertainty, and decision margin.
- Distinguish empirical uncertainty intervals from formal proof status.
- Scope formal properties, assumptions, bounds, equivalence relations, and
  inconclusive outcomes without confusing proof with specification adequacy.
- Diagnose proxy mismatch, confounding, variability, and selection bias before
  treating a reported difference as an architecture result.
- Separate an observed outcome from its proposed mechanism and state the
  coverage, shared assumptions, nonclaims, and consequences that limit it.
- Route feedback to the environment, representation, study, approach, project
  record, or design without turning every result into training data.

:::

## From Tool Return to Feedback {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

Execution and interpretation answer different questions. The environment
records whether a request was valid, what ran, what failed, which artifacts
returned, and what state and cost accompanied the attempt. This chapter begins
after that record exists. It asks whether a returned field measures the
requested quantity, bears on a named property, and can support a comparison or
revision.

Not every feedback source returns a measurement. A review rationale, model
critique, proof status, counterexample, or tool warning may still be useful
when its source, target, scope, timing, and limitations are recorded. A
numerical return needs additional qualification before it can support a
comparison.

A failed setup is not a poor measurement of a candidate. It is no candidate
measurement at all. A clean process exit may still return a partial report,
omit a required field, use the wrong unit, or parse an unfamiliar warning as
success. A complete return can contain a genuine limit violation. Execution
status must survive intact so interpretation can distinguish these cases.

Returned feedback gains meaning only as it passes distinct qualifications
(@fig-evidence-flow). Each completed step adds something the preceding step did
not establish. An incomplete measurement can return directly to execution, and
an invalid comparison can return directly to study formulation.

![**A tool return gains meaning in stages.** The execution record first
supplies a return with status and lineage. Measurement qualification binds a
quantity to a candidate and conditions. A matched comparison adds a
comparator, difference, and uncertainty. A scoped interpretation states what
the result supports and does not support. Qualification failures return to the
environment, comparison failures return to study formulation, and a completed
interpretation records learning and any needed revision.](images/F8-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow
width="88%" fig-alt="A five-step flow from tool return through measurement
qualification and matched comparison to scoped interpretation and
a recorded next step. Side paths send incomplete measurements to the
environment and invalid comparisons to study formulation."}

The execution record supplies a return with status and lineage. Qualification
determines whether a returned field measures a named
quantity for a particular candidate and set of conditions. A matched comparison
then adds the comparator, difference, and uncertainty, after which the scoped
interpretation states what the result supports and what it does not. The final
record may preserve learning, request a revision, or require no change. A
missing execution field routes back to the environment, while an invalid
comparison routes back to study formulation. Feedback becomes useful by
identifying which object needs attention, not by prescribing its own update.

## Sources of Feedback

Human reviewers, architecture tools, learned methods, and deployed systems all
return feedback. Their differences create a coverage tradeoff rather than one
preferred source (@tbl-feedback-sources). No source combines complete context,
immediate response, precise localization, and decision-relevant coverage.

| **Source** | **Common form** | **Timing and locality** | **Main quality question** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Human reviewer** | Critique, rationale, missing constraint, or priority judgment. | Intermittent and often context-rich; locality depends on the review. | Does the reviewer have the relevant context, expertise, and authority, and is the rationale recorded? |
| **Architecture tool or experiment** | Scalar, trace, report, counterexample, diagnostic, or proof status. | Immediate to multi-day; may identify one path or only a terminal outcome. | Which property did the tool observe, under which conditions, with what coverage and error? |
| **Learned model or method** | Prediction, ranking, score, critique, or explanation. | Usually fast and dense; often tied to the supplied representation. | Does the predicted score agree with stronger checks in the region being used, and which assumptions does it share with the producer? |
| **Deployed system or silicon** | Telemetry, characterization result, incident, or user-visible symptom. | Delayed and sparse; often system-level rather than component-local. | Which population, version, workload, and unobserved causes limit the inference? |

: **Feedback sources differ in what they return and how quickly they arrive.**
Quality depends on whether the signal is fit for the learning or revision it is
asked to support.
{#tbl-feedback-sources tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

Human review can carry substantial context but arrives intermittently.
Architecture tools return property-specific values or artifacts whose
conditions and coverage must be recorded. Learned methods return dense signals
whose calibration and shared assumptions need checking. Deployment observes
system behavior directly but supports an inference only after versions,
workloads, and other possible causes are separated. The final column prevents
speed, density, or direct observation from standing in for evidence quality.
Source type alone does not decide whether feedback is fit for a particular
revision.

Delayed feedback can resolve an outcome while teaching little about how to
revise the work. A three-day place-and-route and timing run may show that a
candidate missed timing, but the final result does not identify which of
thousands of generated choices caused the miss. Revision needs a signal at the
right locality, such as path slack linked to the graph node, parameter, or
transformation that changed.

Handling that delayed result begins with lineage rather than causal
attribution. Bind the return to the exact candidate, parent actions, represented
state, constraints, tool and checker versions, seed, checkpoint, workload, and
software conditions that produced it. Lineage alone does not qualify the
return. When execution, setup, extraction, and check conditions are valid, the
terminal result can establish that this candidate missed timing under those
conditions. It does not yet establish which earlier action caused the miss.

The next step is a distinguishing comparison. Inspect path endpoints,
constraint coverage, congestion, power-density maps, and the differences from
the parent or a matched sibling. A stale constraint or broken setup routes the
revision to the environment or representation. Repeated failure across a
matched proposal class, after shared setup and conditions are checked, can
justify reopening the method or study and asking whether the representation,
shared constraints, or proposal process needs to change. A localized mechanism
supported by the comparison can justify a design revision. If no diagnostic
separates those possibilities, preserve the terminal outcome and leave the
mechanism unresolved rather than turning every upstream action into a negative
label.

Deployment feedback follows the same rule. A field result attaches first to the
shipped hardware, software, workload, and operating conditions it observed.
Those conditions may reopen an earlier claim, but the field symptom does not
identify the responsible design choice until an additional comparison or
diagnostic supports that attribution.

Dense, immediate feedback is easier for a method to learn from, but it is often
a proxy. Feedback that observes a decision-relevant property may be slower,
more expensive, or less frequent. Fast proxy signals can guide search only
inside their validated range. Slower or less frequent checks can test
properties the proxy omits. A feedback budget therefore records latency,
granularity, execution cost, uncertainty, interpretation time, and review cost.

## Qualifying Empirical Measurements

An empirical measurement is an observed or computed quantity from a run,
experiment, implementation flow, prototype, or deployed system under recorded
conditions. It may carry sampling variation, run-to-run variability, numerical
tolerance, and model error. Those limits differ from the logical status of a
formal result.

A measurement record needs enough information to answer six questions
(@tbl-measurement-record).

| **Field** | **Question the record must answer** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidate identity** | Which design revision, configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| **Quantity and unit** | What property was measured or computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| **Conditions** | Which tool, model, configuration, corner, seed where relevant, and operating conditions apply? |
| **Extraction status** | Did the expected artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain unfamiliar warnings? |
| **Variation and error** | What repetitions, sampling method, numerical tolerance, model error, or known bound limits the value? |
| **Source record** | Which returned artifact and execution attempt support the field, and can the value be recovered from them? |

: **A measurement is a returned value with identity, meaning, conditions, and
limits.** These fields test whether the execution record is sufficient for the
comparison being attempted.
{#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The first two rows bind the value to a candidate and define the property it
represents. Conditions and extraction status establish whether the requested
field returned under the declared setup. Variation and error bound its
precision, while the source record makes the value recoverable from a specific
attempt and artifact. Completing these fields does not make a comparison
valid. It makes the returned value eligible to enter one.

The environment provides returned artifacts, extraction status, recorded
conditions, and lineage; measurement qualification does not reconstruct
missing versions or rerun a parser. It asks whether the quantity, aggregation,
error, comparator, and check scope make the returned field usable as a
measurement. Missing execution fields require an environment repair.
Inadequate observations or an invalid comparison require a change to the
study.

The Lighthouse record demonstrates three interpretation rules. The clean
returns can illustrate comparison logic, but they must be rerun before they
become independently qualified project measurements. The stale-state attempt
is a setup failure rather than a measurement of the 3\ MB candidate. The
trace's absence of a 4\ MB cycle-level call illustrates a scheduling outcome. A
real study would need retained parser and dispatch evidence before treating
that short-circuit as verified. Missing information remains part of each
result.

This distinction prevents two common errors. An infrastructure failure cannot
become negative training data about a design. A favorable value with unknown
conditions cannot become evidence simply because its unit looks familiar.

Once a value is qualified, it can enter the comparison that the architecture
question requires. Qualification establishes what one return means.
Comparison establishes what differs between the candidate and a declared
alternative under matched conditions.

Empirical uncertainty and formal proof status answer different questions. An
empirical interval summarizes variation under a sampling and repetition
procedure. Its interpretation depends on the population, statistic, dependence
structure, model error, and decision margin. A formal result is not a narrow
empirical interval and has no sampling confidence level. It reports a logical
outcome for a stated property, model, and assumptions. Solver time, proof
depth, and memory limit its scope or completion, not its statistical
confidence.

## Formal Verification and Its Scope

Formal verification begins with three objects. The *property* states the
behavior to check. The *model* defines the state, transitions, and artifacts
over which the property is interpreted. The *assumptions* restrict inputs,
environment behavior, reset, clocks, protocols, or neighboring components. A
formal result is meaningful only when all three travel with it. A proof over
the wrong model or under an impossible assumption can be logically sound and
architecturally useless.

The returned status should distinguish four outcomes:

- **Proved:** A sound proof method established the stated property or
  equivalence relation for the declared model and assumptions. A method need
  not be complete for a proof it successfully returns to be valid.
- **Counterexample:** The tool returned a modeled trace that violates the
  property. The trace still needs setup and assumption review before it is
  treated as a realizable architecture failure.
- **Bounded-only:** No counterexample was found through the declared horizon.
  The result says nothing beyond that bound unless a separate completeness
  argument applies.
- **Inconclusive:** The solver returned `unknown`, exhausted time or memory,
  failed to complete induction, or otherwise supplied no proof or
  counterexample. Resource exhaustion is not partial correctness.

Bounded model checking searches modeled traces through a finite bound \(k\)
under stated assumptions [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Failing to find a counterexample
through \(k\) does not exclude a longer one. An unbounded safety conclusion
requires a completeness argument or an unbounded method such as induction or
IC3/property-directed reachability [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Even
then, the result covers only the stated property over the modeled transition
system and assumptions.

Safety and liveness make different claims. A safety property excludes a bad
behavior, such as two requesters simultaneously holding exclusive ownership of
one cache line. Proving such a safety property without a bound still does not
establish progress. A liveness property requires progress, such as an accepted request eventually
receiving a response [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A bounded response check can expose a slow or stuck
execution within its horizon, but it does not prove that starvation or deadlock
is impossible beyond that horizon. An unbounded progress claim needs a
liveness-capable proof or a justified reduction, and it must retain the
fairness assumptions that rule out indefinitely postponed actions. Unrealistic
fairness assumptions can hide an architectural progress defect. The result
therefore records the property class, fairness assumptions, proof method, and
any bound or reduction used.

A property can pass without checking the intended behavior. *Vacuity* occurs
when a condition that should trigger the property never occurs, so the
implication is always true [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A nonvacuous property can still be weak. It may allow
a response thousands of cycles late, omit exclusivity, ignore reset, or check
one requester while leaving another unconstrained. Teams can exercise
properties with cover statements, reachable triggers, known positive and
negative cases, mutation, and review against the requirement they are meant to
express. Systems such as AssertLLM generate
SystemVerilog assertions from design specifications and evaluate them against
golden RTL with formal property verification [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM]. If the
RTL and assertions inherit the same missing requirement, a clean proof still
says nothing about the omitted behavior.

Equivalence checking asks whether two artifacts preserve a declared relation.
Combinational equivalence compares functions without architectural state.
Sequential equivalence relates state and behavior across time. Retiming,
latency changes, additional state, or a changed reset mapping can make
sequential correspondence much harder than synthesis-oriented comparison.
Neither form establishes that the reference artifact expresses the intended
architecture.

Equivalence is also too strong when an implementation intentionally adds
detail or permits fewer behaviors than an abstract specification. A refinement
check instead asks whether each implementation behavior allowed by the mapping
remains within the specification. Large proofs are often decomposed by
component. In an assume-guarantee argument, each block proves a guarantee only
while its environment satisfies named assumptions; the composition is sound
only when neighboring guarantees discharge those assumptions
[@BenvenisteEtAl2012Contracts]. A block proof does not silently become a
whole-system proof. The refinement mapping, component boundaries, assumptions,
and unproved remainder remain part of the result.

Dynamic simulation makes a different claim. Directed tests,
constrained-random stimuli, coverage-guided generation, emulation, formal
methods, and post-silicon testing complement one another because exhaustive
simulation is generally infeasible. Code coverage reports exercised
structures. Functional coverage reports events or bins defined by the
verification plan. Neither reports the fraction of every reachable behavior
checked, while a formal proof covers no property that was never written.

Published accounts of the Pentium division failure document both the missing
table entries and Intel's \$475 million pretax charge
[@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV bug and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** Pre-silicon testing supported the implemented floating-point
division behavior over the cases it exercised.

**The gap.** Five missing table entries escaped testing and produced incorrect
results for rare operand pairs. Intel later reported a \$475 million pretax
charge for replacement and associated costs.

**The lesson.** Sampled tests cannot support an unbounded absence claim.
Another check is needed when the property demands one.
:::

Formal verification later became the primary validation method for the
execution cluster in Intel's Core i7 flow [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal].

## Making Measurements Comparable {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

Architecture decisions usually depend on differences rather than isolated
values. A cache study asks how a candidate differs from a baseline under the
same workload and software state. Two candidates produced by different
processes can also be compared here, but the result is limited to their
measured design difference rather than the quality of the complete workflows
that produced them. The comparator is part of the claim, not a footnote added
after the result.

A comparison must bind two designs to one measured difference and to the scope
that limits it (@fig-claim-frame).

![**A comparison binds two designs to one measured difference and its
limits.** Candidate and comparator are evaluated for the same quantity and
unit. The result remains conditional on workload and state, tool conditions,
uncertainty, and the property the check can observe.](images/F7-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame
width="100%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate
and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty, which
are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

The candidate and comparator enter as explicit revisions and configurations.
Both feed the same quantity and unit
before the center column states their difference and its uncertainty. The
right-hand column binds that result to workload and design state, tool and
operating conditions, and the check's scope and nonclaims. A different scope
creates a different comparison even when the center value is unchanged.

For matched cases \(c_j\), the basic paired difference is

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j).
$$

The sign convention must be stated. Positive may mean improvement for
throughput and regression for latency. A percentage must name its
denominator. An aggregate must state whether it is a mean, percentile, maximum,
geometric mean, or another statistic. Without those choices, two correct
numbers can still form an incoherent comparison.

### Matching Factors That Can Change the Result

The candidate and comparator should differ only along the factors the study
intends to compare. Workload, software, model version, tool flags, operating
point, warmup, sampling window, and resource budget can all create a
difference that has nothing to do with the architecture change. A matched
comparison records them rather than relying on similar filenames or a shared
directory.

Systematic model error sometimes cancels in a relative comparison. It does so
only when the model treats the candidate and comparator similarly in the
region being studied. A frozen simulator can support an ordering even when its
absolute prediction differs from silicon, but that bargain fails when the
architecture change crosses an unmodeled boundary or affects one candidate
differently. Cancellation is a hypothesis to check, not a property of using
the same tool.

### Differences and Their Uncertainty

Repeated measurements estimate run-to-run variability when the flow or
workload is variable. Paired resampling can preserve the relationship between
matched baseline and candidate frames.[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]
Numerical tolerances, finite sampling, heuristic variation, and model error
may require different treatments. One generic error bar cannot represent all
of them.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]: **Paired block resampling** resamples
matched baseline and candidate observations together in contiguous blocks.
Pairing preserves the comparison, while blocks preserve short-range dependence
among nearby observations under the method's assumptions
[@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].

The constructed trace in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces uses
improvement as baseline
latency minus candidate latency, so a positive value means the candidate is
faster. Under that convention, the illustrative reduction is 0.3\ ms and its
illustrative 95 percent interval runs from -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms, using paired
block resampling over matched frame sequences. Because the interval includes
zero, the comparison does not resolve the declared tail-latency
question. The point estimate is favorable, but its uncertainty spans both a
small regression and a larger improvement. The interval cannot be recomputed
from the constructed record because the matched frame sequences and their
identifiers are not retained. It remains a teaching comparison rather than a
replayed calculation.

A decision margin adds a second test. If the study requires an improvement of
at least \(m\), the comparison must resolve the result relative to \(m\), not
merely relative to zero. A difference inside known measurement resolution or
uncertainty remains unresolved. Calling it a tie may be appropriate under a
predeclared rule, but calling it an improvement is not.

### Controlling Confounding and Selection

A matched comparison can still support the wrong explanation. Confounding
exists when another changed factor could account for the result. Stable
versions, ablations, matched contrasts, and sensitivity studies help separate
the intended change from plausible alternatives.

Selection introduces another problem. If a search evaluates many noisy
candidates and reports only the best, the selected value retains some of the
luck that made it win. Repeating the same search data does not remove that
bias. The chosen candidate should be measured again on fresh seeds, workloads,
or cases that did not select it. The fresh evaluation asks whether the margin
survives after the search has stopped choosing the winner
[@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse].

Even a carefully matched comparison supports nothing beyond the properties
its checks can observe. The next question is therefore not only whether the
candidate and comparator were treated alike, but whether the selected checks
bear on the claim being made.

## Testing Explanations and Proxies {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

An architecture proxy is useful because it is cheaper or earlier than the
quantity that ultimately matters. Estimated IPC, analytical energy, wirelength,
congestion, utilization, and cycle counts can all help order candidates. They
remain partial measurements. The danger grows when an optimizer searches
directly against them, because the search is rewarded for finding every region
where the proxy and the intended result part company.

This is Goodhart's problem in architecture form. A measure that once tracked a
goal can stop tracking it after it becomes the optimization target
[@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. AI is not unique in
this behavior. It changes the scale and persistence of the search for
loopholes.

Support coverage and held-out agreement answer separate questions
(@fig-trust-calibration). The conceptual schematic uses normalized quantities
rather than measured data. Its shaded support region says only where matched
calibration cases exist. Held-out error, ranking stability, and uncertainty
relative to the decision margin determine whether the proxy is usable even
inside that region. Outside it, the relationship is extrapolated and may
diverge.

![**Observed support is necessary but does not establish calibration
accuracy.** The normalized curves illustrate one case where a proxy tracks a
stronger reference over an observed support region and diverges under
continued search. A real study must establish both support coverage and
held-out agreement.](images/F9-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%"
fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot. A proxy and stronger reference track in an
observed support region, then may diverge outside it as optimization continues.
A label states that support does not establish held-out agreement."}

Within the shaded region, matched cases establish that the proxy and reference
have both been observed; held-out comparisons must still show whether their
errors and candidate ordering are adequate for the decision. Continued search
beyond that support turns the relationship into extrapolation, where the two
curves may separate. The widening gap illustrates why a higher proxy score
cannot be treated as a stronger result without new reference checks.

Six problems should be tested separately (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare the proxy with a more decision-relevant measurement on matched cases. | The proxy result cannot carry the stronger claim. |
| **Support coverage** | Place matched calibration cases across the workloads and candidate region the search visits. | The reported candidate lies in unsupported extrapolation. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error, ranking stability, and uncertainty against the decision margin on cases not used to fit or tune the proxy. | The proxy cannot reliably order candidates even without extrapolation. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed, use matched contrasts, and test plausible alternative causes. | The difference does not identify the proposed cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows or sampled workloads and report dispersion or ranking stability. | The point estimate may not resolve the declared margin. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate the selected candidate on fresh cases not used to choose it. | The apparent margin may contain the luck that made the candidate win. |

: **Each weakness requires a different diagnostic.** A second run cannot repair
a missing property, and a stronger tool cannot repair an unmatched comparator.
{#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[18,43,39]"}

The first three rows test whether the proxy observes the relevant property,
covers the region the search visits, and orders held-out cases reliably inside
that region. The next three separate alternative causes, run-to-run variation,
and the favorable noise retained when a search selects its winner. The final
column states which inference an adverse result removes. One failed diagnostic
does not make the other diagnoses or their repairs interchangeable.

The public debate over learned macro placement illustrates why calibration and
matched comparison matter. Proxy metrics such as wirelength and congestion do
not automatically settle post-route power, performance, and area, and public
assessments have differed in tool flow, baseline strength, pretraining, and
available design data [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. The durable lesson is
not a verdict on one placement method. It is that a proxy comparison cannot
silently inherit strength from a stronger result obtained under unmatched
conditions.

A simulator can also be the exploited reference. In Gupta et al.'s
architecture-agent study, a ChampSim assertion against last-level-cache write
bypass was eliminated by the optimized build, so that configuration did not
enforce the intended correctness constraint [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent].
Calibration to that run would reproduce the blind spot. The reference check
must itself retain the property, configuration, and coverage used to justify
it.

### Separating the Outcome From the Mechanism

An outcome says what changed. A mechanism says why. They require different
comparisons and can reach different statuses.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A lower miss count is not the architecture result"}
For the Lighthouse cache study, the reported outcome question concerns
99th-percentile frame time. The mechanism question asks whether added capacity
reduces capacity misses and whether that reduction explains a tail-latency
change. The 12 percent miss reduction supports the reported intermediate
effect within the cache model. It does not prove that the miss reduction caused
a tail frame-time change. The frame-time interval crosses zero, so the intended
performance outcome remains unresolved.
:::

The reverse can also occur. A candidate may improve the measured outcome while
the proposed explanation fails. The improvement can remain a valid observation
if the comparison is sound, but an unresolved or contradicted mechanism should
not guide the next change. A plausible model explanation is a hypothesis, not
a substitute for a contrast.

Useful mechanism checks include matched workload contrasts, ablations,
counterfactual configurations, traces of the affected events, and sensitivity
around the changed parameter. They should be declared before the result when
possible. Otherwise, an explanation can be fitted to any outcome after the
fact. The resulting judgments must remain separate even when they come from
the same study (@tbl-outcome-mechanism).

| **Question** | **Possible status** | **Lighthouse illustration** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Did the requested quantity change in the declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved within the stated comparison. | Tail frame-time improvement remains unresolved because the interval includes zero. |
| **Did the proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or not tested. | Capacity misses are reported 12 percent lower for the clean 3\ MB return group. |
| **Did that intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by a distinguishing contrast; otherwise unresolved. | The causal link between fewer misses and tail latency remains unresolved. |
| **What did the check not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | No result establishes thermal behavior, voltage-droop behavior, functional correctness, security, or system-level XR quality. |

: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results.** A supported intermediate
effect cannot fill an unresolved architecture comparison.
{#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[26,30,44]"}

The four rows cover the observed outcome, the reported intermediate effect,
the causal explanation, and the properties no check observed. The first two
may resolve without the third, while the final
row prevents a local cache result from becoming a claim about thermal,
electrical, functional, security, or system behavior.

This separation makes negative results useful. A contradicted mechanism can
improve the architecture model even when the candidate result is favorable. A
resolved regression can rule out a design direction. An unresolved comparison
can reveal that the observation budget or measurement plan was too weak. None
of those outcomes is a failed study if the record keeps them distinct.

The 4\ MB line deserves care. Accepting the illustrative values as given, its
reported area and access time fail the declared checks, so 4\ MB is rejected
from `XR-L2-CAP-A` and no cycle-level call is spent. The surviving record is not
strong enough to independently replay that interpretation because the parser
and dispatch evidence is missing. The bounded rejection also does not apply to
every future study. A new memory compiler, PVT point, area budget, or
access-time target changes the comparison.

The 3\ MB line shows why passing several checks does not settle an architecture
question. The physical-model values meet their local limits. The reported
intermediate effect is favorable. The causal mechanism and intended
tail-latency outcome remain unresolved. Each statement is useful because none
is allowed to impersonate the others.

## Scope, Uncertainty, and Assurance {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

Assurance is a structured account of a result, not one confidence score. It
names the property and scope, check coverage and possible error direction,
shared assumptions, formal proof status where applicable, empirical and model
uncertainty, the basis for any independence claim, explicit nonclaims, and the
consequence of being wrong. These fields cannot be averaged into one number.
A proved property can coexist with uncertain performance, incomplete workload
coverage, and an untested security claim.

Some architecture results depend on confidential workloads, design data, or
tool flows. They can support an internal conclusion when an authorized reviewer
can inspect the complete record and challenge its method, scope, uncertainty,
and limits. A public claim must remain within what public material or an audit
by a reviewer with access to the protected record can establish.
Confidentiality does not turn a production report into an independently
replayable comparison.

### What Different Checks Establish

A valid measurement may still address the wrong property. Syntax checks,
functional simulation, model checking, performance simulation, synthesis,
timing analysis, power analysis, and post-silicon characterization answer
different questions. Their strength is not a single ordering from weak to
strong. A parser can conclusively reject an illegal request while an expensive
timing run says nothing about functional correctness. Representative check
boundaries make that mismatch explicit without implying a universal ordering
(@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What it can support within stated conditions** | **What it does not establish by itself** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Syntax and interface** | Legal encoding, type, schema, ISA, ABI, or protocol form. | Functional behavior, performance, physical feasibility, or system intent. |
| **Functional simulation and testing** | Behavior for exercised stimuli and observed properties. | Unexercised behaviors, physical timing, power, or unspecified security properties. |
| **Formal property and equivalence checks** | A stated property over a modeled transition system, or a stated relation between two artifacts. | Whether the property captures intent, whether assumptions match deployment, or unrelated properties. |
| **Architecture performance and power models** | Quantities represented by the model for the declared workload and configuration. | Effects the abstraction omits or behavior outside its validated region. |
| **Implementation and physical analysis** | Timing, area, power, integrity, or rule results for the modeled design, constraints, modes, and corners. | Missing constraints, unmodeled conditions, functional intent, or manufactured variation outside the analysis. |
| **Post-silicon and operational measurement** | Behavior of sampled parts and systems under measured conditions. | Every manufactured part, workload, environment, lifetime condition, or unmeasured property. |

: **A check is decisive only for the property it observes.** More cost or later
placement in a flow does not widen that property.
{#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The rows cover changes in observed property, not a universal ranking. Syntax
checks establish form. Simulation and formal checks observe
specified behavior, architecture and physical models cover quantities their
abstractions represent, and post-silicon measurement samples deployed
behavior. The final column names what remains unobserved at each row. A later
or more expensive check can leave an earlier property entirely untouched.

The property a check observes is only half of the measurement plan. The
intended use of its result also matters. A mistaken local ranking can waste
evaluation budget and change which candidates the search examines. A mistaken
result used to revise a shared artifact or interface can propagate across
hardware, software, verification, and integration work. The feedback plan
should therefore grow with the cost of being wrong and the difficulty of
reversing the result's technical consequences
(@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of the result** | **Consequence if the result is wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Choose the next local evaluation** | A candidate is explored unnecessarily, a promising one is deferred, or scarce tool time is spent on the wrong question. | Candidate identity, a matched comparator, known proxy limits, and enough precision to choose the next check. |
| **Revise a shared implementation or interface** | Hardware, software, verification, or integration work may inherit the error. | Relevant regression and compatibility checks, explicit shared assumptions, and a different check path for critical properties where practical. |
| **Support a high-consequence technical conclusion** | The error may survive into later work where it is expensive to find or reverse. | Checks covering each material claim, uncertainty relative to the decision margin, a sufficiently different path where shared failure matters, and explicit unmeasured properties. |

: **The feedback plan follows consequence and reversibility.** More costly
checks are not automatically more informative; the plan must cover the claims
and failure modes that matter for the result's intended use. This technical
assessment does not authorize the resulting action.
{#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[27,32,41]"}

The rows widen the intended use from choosing the next local evaluation, to
revising a shared implementation or interface, to supporting a
high-consequence technical conclusion. A local choice needs candidate identity,
a matched comparator, known proxy limits, and enough precision to choose the
next check. A shared revision adds regression and compatibility checks. A
high-consequence conclusion adds coverage for each material claim, uncertainty
relative to the decision margin, and a sufficiently different path where
shared failure matters. This progression raises the evidence burden. It does
not authorize the resulting action.

### Describing the Check and Its Limits

Three questions that many tool reports omit make a check reviewable.

**Coverage.** Which failures can the check observe, and which relevant failures
leave no signal?

**Possible error direction.** Under the declared model and conditions, is the
result known to be conservative, optimistic, or neither? This must be
established for the particular flow. A pre-route estimate is not always
optimistic, and a deterministic computation is not automatically a safe
bound.

Static timing analysis illustrates why the error direction is conditional. A
result may be deliberately pessimistic, but that claim applies only to the
declared timing mode, process, voltage, and temperature corner, derates,
constraints, and modeled effects. A pass or failure is meaningful within those
conditions, not as a universal bound. Sampled simulation has a different
shape. A failing trace rejects the exercised behavior, but a passing sample
says nothing about unexercised stimuli or properties absent from the testbench.

**Shared assumptions.** Which specifications, models, data, workloads,
constraints, code, and tool paths are shared with the producer or with another
check? A different program name or model instance does not create
independence.

Agreement adds information only when the second path changes the relevant
failure source (@fig-independent-checks). The alternative need not claim
perfect independence. It must observe the disputed property through a
sufficiently different path to reduce a known shared failure.

![**A second check adds information only when it changes the relevant failure
path.** A critic using the same assumptions can repeat the producer's omission.
A claim-specific check based on a sufficiently different model or measurement
path can reduce that correlation, but its remaining shared inputs and blind
spots must still be recorded.](images/ch7_independent_checks){#fig-independent-checks
width="92%" fig-alt="Two-column diagram. A producer and
critic sharing the same assumptions lead to correlated agreement. A producer
and a claim-specific check with a different measurement path lead to a
bounded challenge, with remaining shared assumptions explicitly retained."}

In the left path, the candidate producer and critic use the same specification
and model, so agreement remains correlated. In the right path, a claim-specific
check observes the disputed property differently and produces a bounded
challenge. The note beneath both
paths sets the limit. Some assumptions and inputs may remain shared, so a
different path can reduce correlation without proving independence.

Two uses of a second path should not be conflated. Independent qualification
of the same record challenges extraction, arithmetic, or bookkeeping. A
separate parser can recover a value from the raw report, and an independent
calculation can check its aggregation. Both may still inherit the original
tool's model, workload, and constraints. They strengthen confidence in what
that tool returned without testing whether the tool observed the right
physical property.

A materially different observation path challenges more of the claim. Another
simulator with different models, an RTL property check, a physical-design
measurement, or a direct hardware observation may expose an error that record
requalification cannot. It also has shared assumptions that must be named.
The useful question is not whether the second path deserves the label
*independent*. It is which failure source changes and which one remains shared.

Separate teams can fail together on the same hard inputs. Knight and Leveson
found correlated failures among independently developed program versions,
showing that separate implementation does not guarantee independent error
[@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. The same warning applies to a generator and
critic that share a foundation model, training data, objective, or
specification. Agreement can be useful corroboration without being an
independent check.

The missing-property case is different. Spectre and Meltdown exploited
microarchitectural side effects that ordinary functional correctness does not
constrain [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. More functional
tests of ordinary program outputs would not settle confidentiality. Tests
designed around leakage can bear on the security claim, while an ordinary
performance suite cannot.

Checks also need checks. Mutation testing injects faults and reports which ones
a suite detects [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. A mutation score says
something only about the injected fault model, and equivalent or unobservable
mutants need careful handling. For AI-authored assertions and testbenches, the
useful fault set should resemble errors the generator actually makes rather
than only traditional hand-written mistakes.

A check can be valid for the property it observes and still be only a proxy
for the architecture objective. Functional simulation may establish agreement
for tested inputs without settling performance, while a cycle estimate may
rank candidates without establishing timing closure. The remaining question
is how far the cheaper observation can carry the stronger claim.

## Feedback That Changes the Work

Feedback does not prescribe its own update. Project learning and model learning
are different. A design constraint, contradicted comparison, supported
intermediate effect, or supported mechanism can update project state without
becoming training data. A model update needs a named target, usable labels,
scope, and acceptance test. Tool failures, unmatched results, and unresolved
comparisons should not become simple pass or fail labels.

An updated model or proxy is a new component version within the design system
[@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. Before it reenters the design process, the project
records the update data and the acquisition policy that selected them. It then
tests failure-relevant cases and prior support groups that were not used for
the update, repeats the decision-relevant error, ranking, or calibration
checks, and looks for regressions over the previously supported region. The
updated component remains outside the active process when it fails these
checks. When it passes, it reenters with revised support and reopening
conditions rather than inheriting the previous version's scope.

Some failed checks can remain open under a bounded waiver accepted by an
authorized owner. The waiver does not turn the failed result into a pass. It
retains the failed check, rationale, exact scope, responsible owner,
compensating check or control, residual risk, expiration or review condition,
and reopening trigger. Waiver support in a physical-verification flow can
preserve waived design-rule violations and their associated text. Siemens
documents this behavior for Calibre Auto-Waivers, which applies the records
across later DRC runs [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. The technical record belongs
here. Authority to accept the residual risk belongs to
@sec-what-architect-owns.

Feedback should update the object whose defect or status it actually
establishes (@tbl-feedback-destinations).

| **What the feedback establishes** | **Update destination** | **Resulting move** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The execution record is incomplete or invalid. | Tool-connected environment | Repair extraction, state, lineage, or invocation before interpreting the candidate. |
| The represented state or dependency is wrong. | Design representation | Correct the represented problem and invalidate results that used the wrong state. |
| A qualified architecture effect is observed. | Project record; design owner if revision is supported | Record the bounded result and revise the design only when the result supports that move. |
| A proxy leaves its support or shows systematic error. | Approach choice or calibration study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or stop using the proxy. Do not create training labels automatically. |
| Human review exposes a missing constraint or assumption. | Study formulation or representation | Record the rationale and revise the object that omitted the requirement. |
| The outcome is resolved but its proposed mechanism is not. | Study formulation | Preserve the result and add a distinguishing contrast before using the explanation to guide another change. |
| The comparison remains unresolved. | Measurement plan or study formulation | Improve the contrast, precision target, observation budget, or stopping rule. |
| A matched comparison resolves that any difference is smaller than the declared decision margin. | Project record | Preserve the result without forcing a design or model update. |
| A qualified failed check is accepted as a bounded exception. | Project record and responsible owner | Preserve the failed status, waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, residual risk, expiration, and reopening condition. |

: **The update follows what the feedback established.** A signal may repair the
environment, representation, approach, study, or design, and a valid result may
require no change.
{#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[32,25,43]"}

Incomplete execution returns to the environment, wrong represented state
returns to the representation, and proxy error returns to the approach or its
calibration study. Missing constraints, unresolved mechanisms, and unresolved
comparisons reopen the study or measurement plan. Qualified effects and
differences below the decision margin may update only the project record. A
waiver preserves a failed check as a scoped exception rather than relabeling it.
No route turns a tool failure or unresolved comparison into a training label
automatically.

Reopening marks the conditions under which an old interpretation no longer
applies. A changed workload, software image, model, tool, operating condition,
candidate revision, calibration result, or contrary observation can reopen the
result without predetermining the next revision. Monitoring should distinguish
three kinds of change. Claim-binding identities and execution conditions can
make the old record stale. Workload populations or phase coverage can leave
the earlier sample unsupported. Proxy-reference residuals or ranking stability
can show that a cheap check no longer tracks the stronger reference. A trigger
marks the prior interpretation for requalification. It does not automatically
revise the design or retrain a model. Cross-problem transfer belongs to
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, while evaluation of the complete monitoring
and recovery behavior belongs to @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

## Open Research Questions

The open problems begin where current tools stop supplying the interpretation
fields automatically.

### Qualifying Returned Feedback and Checks

**How should an unfamiliar returned field be qualified before it supports a
measurement or revision?** The evaluator must recover its producer, target,
unit, conditions, and limits without silently treating an unrecognized value
as a familiar metric.

**How should shared failure sources be measured across checks?** Separate
tools, models, teams, and modalities can still share specifications, workloads,
training data, libraries, or assumptions that create correlated error.

**Which mutations test AI-authored verification collateral?** Traditional
fault models may not resemble the semantic omissions, weak assertions, or
misinterpreted interfaces that generated tests and properties introduce.

**How can a formal campaign detect weak but nonvacuous properties?** A
property may trigger and pass while omitting required timing, exclusivity,
reset, or interaction behavior. Useful diagnostics must expose that missing
strength without assuming the implementation is the specification.

### Allocating Costly Measurements and Validating Proxies

**How can a proxy's validated region be estimated under active search?** The
candidate distribution changes as the optimizer learns where the proxy is most
favorable, which is exactly where previous calibration data may be thinnest.

**How should scarce high-cost measurements be allocated?** The useful next
check is the one whose possible outcomes can resolve the comparison, narrow
its scope, or distinguish competing mechanisms, not simply the next tool in a
fixed sequence. Before the check runs, its information value is uncertain,
its outcomes depend on the candidate, and its cost and failure sources may not
match those of the alternatives.

### Learning From Unresolved or Conflicting Results

**How can credit be assigned without inventing a mechanism?** Long architecture
flows return sparse outcomes after many interacting changes, while localized
diagnostics can be correlated with the proxy that selected the candidate.

**How should conflicting feedback be reconciled?** A reviewer, learned
critique, simulator, physical tool, and field observation may disagree because
they see different properties or conditions. The record must preserve those
scope differences before the project treats one source as decisive.

## Conclusion {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Useful feedback carries its source, scope, and limits"}
Feedback can guide learning only when the record names its producer, target,
meaning, timing, scope, and quality limits. Dense proxy feedback can guide local
revision inside its validated range. Less frequent feedback can test
decision-relevant properties the proxy omits. Neither supports an update beyond
what it actually observed.
:::

The central boundary is not probabilistic AI on one side and deterministic
truth on the other. It is the boundary between producing a candidate and
checking a named property through a separate, qualified path. Generators can
be deterministic. Verification tools can be heuristic, randomized, sampled,
or model-dependent. What matters is whether the check observes the property,
under which conditions, with what uncertainty, and with which shared
assumptions.

Empirical and formal returns preserve different status. An empirical interval
summarizes variation under a declared sampling and repetition procedure. A
formal result records whether a property was proved, violated by a
counterexample, checked only to a bound, or left inconclusive for a stated
model and assumptions. Neither result widens itself. Coverage, specification
adequacy, model error, and unchecked properties remain visible.

The Lighthouse example makes the discipline concrete. A stale-state attempt is
an execution failure, not a design measurement. Reported physical-model values
can clear local limits without settling tail performance. A 12 percent miss
reduction can support an intermediate effect inside the cache model while the
causal mechanism and frame-time improvement remain unresolved. Missing
artifacts and conditions remain missing even when the teaching conclusion is
clear.

The cumulative study record therefore carries the feedback source, target,
form, timing and locality, scope, quality limits, status, and update
destination. A measurement also carries the candidate and comparator,
quantity and conditions, difference and uncertainty, check scope and shared
assumptions, outcome and mechanism status, nonclaims, and reopening
conditions. Those fields let the project repair the environment,
representation, study, approach, or design while preserving the valid result
that requires no change. They do not turn unresolved feedback into a pass,
fail, or training label.

The constructed cache trace isolates the difference between a returned value
and qualified feedback. A different retained run is needed to show how those
distinctions survive execution, review, and handoff from formulation through
judgment (@sec-running-the-loop).
